newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EMU criteria must be strictly followed - Duisenberg.
newsitem.headline: EMU criteria must be strictly followed - Duisenberg.

text.p: A strict interpretation of the convergence criteria in the Maastricht Treaty is essential to the viability of European economic and monetary union, Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Friday.

He said the loss of the ability to adjust exchanges rates between European countries was sometimes seen as one of the main disadvantages of the process which creates a single European currency, the euro.
Addressing a conference, Duisenberg said the chances of "asymmetrical shocks" arising which would require exchange rates to be adjusted were a matter of "crystal ball gazing".

"Nevertheless, I believe it is this very factor which underscores why strict interpretation of the convergence criteria contained in the Maastricht Treaty is essential to the viability of monetary union," he told the ABN AMRO conference on "Convergence of Three Economic World Powers".

"If countries are admitted to EMU only when they have sufficiently converged, the chances of asymmetrical shocks within EMU are reduced to a minimum. Relinquishing the exchange rate instrument is then not the disadvantage it is sometimes held to be at first glance."
Duisenberg takes over on July 1 as head of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner of the European Central Bank, which will run monetary policy under EMU from 1999.
He also said proponents of the view that the stability pact would lead to the relinquishment of budgetary policy as an instrument of stabilisation did not fully understand how the pact worked.
The pact aims to ensure that fiscal discipline will be maintained, after EMU begins, among member countries adopting the single European currency.
He said the pact boosted discipline by way of the explicit agreement that EMU member states must, on average, strive for a budget close to balance or in surplus.
Duisenberg also denied that the pact would sap budgetary policy of all flexibility, leaving only a rigid structure incapable of absorbing cyclical adversity.
"If, in times of boom, (EMU) member states record budget surpluses, they will be very well placed to cope adequately with cyclical adversity," he said.
"I am firmly convinced that if public finances are sound, the stability pact will prove flexible enough," he added.
